meaning: Third king of Israel, builder of the Temple

phonemes.desc: Voiceless postalveolar fricative [ʃ] — Hebrew shin, marked by the upper right dot — with a short vocal sheva [ə].
Lateral approximant [l] followed by long [oː], the holam under ל.
Bilabial nasal [m] plus long [oː], the holam under מ; the final ה is silent, a mater lectionis for the long vowel.

pronunciation.approximation: 'shuh-LOH-moh' — start with a quick 'shuh'; both later 'o' sounds are long and steady, like 'show'.

kin.label: Hebrew root
kin.form: š-l-m, 'to be whole, complete, at peace' — the name is a qal passive participle or noun form

kin.label: Arabic
kin.form: Sulaymān (سُلَيْمَان), a distinct but etymologically related form from the same s-l-m root

pronunciation.note: BHS points the name שְׁלֹמֹה (1 Kings 1:1). The initial shewa is vocal (šəwa naʿ) because it opens the word; the two holams are long [oː]. The final he is silent. Modern Israeli Hebrew flattens the vowels to [o] and often elides the shewa, but the Tiberian tradition distinguishes length. HALOT s.v. שְׁלֹמֹה; TDOT s.v. Solomon.

domains.title: Builder of the Temple
domains.subtitle: Sage, Trader, Judge
domains.lead: Šəlōmōh is the king who turns peace into architecture. Son of David, he inherits a united kingdom and spends it on cedar, gold, and wisdom. His Temple in Jerusalem becomes the fixed center of Israelite worship; his judgment becomes proverbial; his trade fleets reach the edges of the known world. Yet his story ends in fracture: the kingdom he built splits the moment he dies.

cards.name: The Temple
cards.desc: A house of cedar, stone, and gold for the name of YHWH, built with Phoenician artisans and dedicated with fire and cloud (1 Kings 6–8).

cards.name: Wisdom and Judgment
cards.desc: His prayer at Gibeon asks for wisdom, and his famous verdict — to cut the disputed child in two — reveals the true mother (1 Kings 3).

cards.name: Fleet and Trade
cards.desc: A navy at Ezion-Geber and an alliance with Hiram of Tyre bring gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks from Ophir (1 Kings 9–10).

cards.name: Proverbs and Song
cards.desc: Tradition ascribes to him the books of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs — wisdom literature that ranges from proverb to eros to despair.

symbols.name: Temple
symbols.meaning: The fixed house of YHWH in Jerusalem, the center of Israelite cult and identity

symbols.name: Seal / signet
symbols.meaning: The legendary ring that commanded demons and animals in later Jewish and Islamic folklore

symbols.name: Scales
symbols.meaning: The instrument of his wise judgment and the balance of peace (šālôm)

symbols.name: Peacock and gold
symbols.meaning: The exotic wealth of his international trade and the opulence of his court

symbols.name: Crown
symbols.meaning: The throne of ivory overlaid with gold and the apex of Israelite royal power

mythology.lead: Šəlōmōh's mythology is the story of wisdom tested by excess. He begins with a prayer for understanding and ends with idolatrous shrines built for his foreign wives. His reign is Israel's golden age and its cautionary tale at once.

myths.title: The Dream at Gibeon
myths.text: When Solomon becomes king — after David's death and Adonijah's failed bid — God appears to him at Gibeon, at the great high place where the king has gone to sacrifice, and offers whatever he asks. Solomon does not ask for riches, long life, or the death of his enemies, but for 'an understanding mind, to discern between good and evil, to govern your people' (1 Kings 3:9; cf. 2 Chronicles 1). Pleased, God grants the wisdom and adds wealth and honor besides, on condition that the king walk in his ways. The story is quietly economic: God offers a blank check, and the king requests an instrument rather than a prize — a 'listening heart' rather than the things a listening heart can win. It became the template for every later legend in which Solomon's wisdom, and not his gold, is the true treasury of Israel, and it frames the whole account that follows: everything magnificent in chapters 3–10 is bonus, granted to a man who asked only to understand.

myths.title: The Judgment of the Two Mothers
myths.text: Two prostitutes of the same house come before the king, each claiming the living newborn, one child having died in the night. Solomon orders a sword: 'Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one and half to the other.' The first woman, whose heart breaks, pleads: 'Give her the living child, and by no means kill him.' The second: 'It shall be neither mine nor yours; divide it.' Solomon gives the child to the first — 'she is his mother' (1 Kings 3:16–27). The verdict works because it converts a dispute of claims into an experiment in love: the false mother proves herself by consenting to the division, the true mother by her willingness to lose. 'And all Israel heard of the judgment... and they perceived that the wisdom of God was in him' (3:28). The myth's enduring afterlife in law and proverb — a 'judgment of Solomon' now means any decision that exposes the truth by accepting the risk of loss — shows how completely the experiment succeeded.

myths.title: The Building and Dedication of the Temple
myths.text: Solomon contracts with Hiram of Tyre for cedar and cypress and for Huram-Abi, 'a craftsman endued with understanding,' and the house rises on the threshing floor of Araunah: an outer court, the hekhal with its cedar carvings of gourds and flowers, and the debir — the holy of holies, twenty cubits square — where two cherubim of olive wood, overlaid with gold, spread their wings over the ark (1 Kings 6–7). Seven years in the building. At the dedication, fire descends and the glory-cloud fills the house, so that the priests cannot stand to minister (8:10–11); Solomon kneels on a bronze platform and prays the longest prayer in the Bible (8:22–53), asking God to hear from heaven when Israel is defeated, drought-stricken, sick, or exiled — and even when 'a foreigner, who is not of your people Israel,' prays toward this house. The first temple is consecrated with its own failure already written into the liturgy, and the stranger's prayer written into its address list.

myths.title: The Queen of Sheba
myths.text: The queen of Sheba journeys to Jerusalem with a caravan of spices, gold, and precious stones — 'a very great retinue' — to test Solomon with hard questions, the chidôt that were the sport of ancient courts (1 Kings 10:1–13; 2 Chronicles 9). He answers all of them; 'nothing was hidden from the king that he could not explain.' She sees the house he built, the fare of his table, the burnt offerings at the Temple, the attendants in their linen, and his cupbearers, and she is left breathless: 'the half was not told me — your wisdom and prosperity surpass the report that I heard,' and blessed be his God. Her gifts and his counter-gifts of 'every desirable thing' mark the southern trade route as a channel of legend — and the chapter's famous inventory, 120 talents of gold a year (roughly four and a half tons), a throne of ivory overlaid with pure gold with twelve lions on its six steps, apes and peacocks arriving by the fleet-load, is the Old Testament's portrait of an economy of reputation: the whole known world audited Jerusalem and found it solvent.

myths.title: The Fall and the Divided Kingdom
myths.text: In his old age the heart of the king was turned — 700 wives, princesses, and 300 concubines, from Moab, Ammon, Edom, Sidon, and the Hittite lands, 'and his wives turned away his heart after other gods' (1 Kings 11:1–8). On the Mount of Olives, east of the city, he built high places for Chemosh of Moab, for Milcom of the Ammonites, and for Astarte of the Sidonians — the builder of the house of YHWH raising shrines within sight of it. The prophet Ahijah of Shiloh tears his new cloak into twelve pieces: ten for Jeroboam the official, one left for David's line 'that my servant David may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem' (11:29–36). The scandal is entirely domestic, and the sentence immediate — the empire outlives its builder by minutes, and no invader is blamed. The narrative makes Solomon the Bible's most successful cautionary tale: he got everything the Gibeon dream offered and withheld, and the story locates the kingdom's fracture not in any army but in the king's divided heart.

lore.syncretism: In Islam, Solomon is Sulaymān, a prophet who commands the wind, speaks with birds, and rules over jinn under God's permission (Qur'an 27). Jewish tradition expands him into a master of demons, a magician-king whose seal controls spirits. Christianity sees him as a type of Christ the wise king and builder of a spiritual temple. Ethiopian legend makes him the father of Menelik I through the Queen of Sheba, founding the Solomonic dynasty claimed by Ethiopian emperors into the twentieth century. The figure of Solomon thus drifts from history into legend, from king into archetype.
lore.culturalLegacy: Šəlōmōh gave the world the idea of the wise king whose wealth is justified by understanding. The 'judgment of Solomon' has entered legal and popular language as a decision that exposes truth by risking loss. The Temple he built remains the imagined heart of Jerusalem, mourned in Jewish liturgy and yearned for in apocalyptic expectation. His attributed writings — Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs — are among the most read books of the Bible, while the Seal of Solomon became a protective amulet across Jewish, Christian, and Islamic magic. In modern archaeology, Solomon is also a battleground: the dating of Iron Age monumental gates at Megiddo, Hazor, and Gezer is central to debates about the historicity and scale of his kingdom.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Šəlōmōh is the king who gets exactly what he asks for and then loses himself in what he does not need. His wisdom is real — it cuts through lies and builds a temple — but it cannot protect him from his own appetites. In that, he is a mirror for every culture that confuses accumulation with meaning.

The Temple he builds is beautiful, yet its completion already contains the warning that no building can house the infinite. When the cloud fills the house, it is a sign not of possession but of presence that exceeds architecture. Solomon's legacy is therefore double: he is the builder of a house and the proof that houses, however splendid, cannot save the builder. To remember him is to ask what we are building, and whether our wisdom is strong enough to refuse what our power can take.

sources.name: Kitchen, On the Reliability of the Old Testament

lore.archaeology: The Temple Mount in Jerusalem, now the Haram al-Sharif, is the traditional site of Solomon's Temple, though no Iron Age remains have been excavated there for religious and political reasons. Monumental six-chambered gates at Megiddo, Hazor, and Gezer have been attributed by some to Solomon's building program, while others date them later to the Omride dynasty. The site of Khirbet Qeiyafa and the Stepped Stone Structure in the City of David are debated as evidence of an early Judahite state. Saba (Sheba) in modern Yemen, with its dam and inscriptions at Marib, confirms the existence of the South Arabian kingdom that the Queen of Sheba legend reflects.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Hebrew name is written שְׁלֹמֹה: the initial shin carries a vocal sheva, and the two occurrences of lamed and mem carry long holam vowels. The final he is silent, serving only as a mater lectionis for the last long o. PUNICODEX renders the name as Šəlōmōh, using the caron on š for the Hebrew shin and macrons to mark the long Tiberian holams. This Latin transcription is registrable as a domain while preserving the consonantal skeleton and vowel length of the Masoretic Text.
